en: Thereafter, in that dust-mandala or in a mandala [drawn] on cloth and so forth—whether it has been directly perceived or is mental—one should perform the consecration of images and the like, preceded by the aforementioned worship and other rites, just as one performs the consecration of a disciple.

Then, having manifested the mandala—whether it be a mandala of colored powders, a painted cloth mandala, or a mental mandala—one should perform the consecration of images and so forth, preceded by the offerings and other rites as previously explained, just like the consecration of a disciple.

Therein, within the mandala as well, having first performed the consecration and placement of the vases according to the previously stated procedure, one should contemplate the image and so forth—produced from the seed-syllables following emptiness or instantaneously in the form of the *samayasattva* together with its seed-syllable—and then cover it with a new red cloth and provide it with flowers.
Having done so...

Furthermore, in other mandalas as well, having first performed the consecration (*adhivāsana*) and installation (*nyāsa*) of the vase according to the previously explained ritual, one should visualize the physical form and so forth—whether completed from the seed-syllable (*bīja*) following the stage of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), or even instantaneously—as being the essence of the commitment-being (*samayasattva*) together with the seed-syllable at the heart. Then, one should cover it with new red cloth or the like and provide it with flowers.
Taking his flower garland, the patron, together with the image and so forth, should enter any one of the mandalas, such as the colored-powder mandala, like a disciple.
Then, having taken this flower garland, the patron, together with the image and so forth, should enter any suitable mandala, such as the colored-powder mandala, like a disciple.
The preceptor, however, should cause a flower to be placed upon the sign of the presiding deity, such as an image,
or upon the sign of the lord of that family.

Then, outside the mandala house in the eastern direction—or if there is no space there, in the northeast, not too far away—in a pleasing location, one should prepare a bathing altar (*snānavedi*). It should be provided with radiance, measuring half the size of the powder-mandala (*rajomaṇḍala*), half as high, square, free from defects such as thorns, and made of clay, brick, or whatever materials are available in their absence; or else, on the ground as it naturally lies, one should draw the altar with plaster and the like, with eight jars placed in the cardinal and intermediate directions.

Having had it cleaned with earth, smeared with the five products of the cow mixed with nectar and other substances, and made beautiful according to one's means with canopies, white umbrellas, banners, flags, full water-jars, flowers, dance, song, instrumental music, and so forth;

Then, outside the mandala house, in the eastern direction—or if that is not possible, in the northeast—in a pleasant location not too far away, one should prepare a bathing platform with a radius equal to half the size of the mandala and a height equal to half of that; it should be constructed from materials such as earth or stone, free from defects such as impurities.

It should be made of materials such as clay or, if those are unavailable, from whatever base is at hand; it may be drawn with a paste of rice-flour and so forth. Upon this platform, eight vases are placed in the cardinal and intermediate directions. It must be exceedingly soft, smeared with the five products of the cow and other substances mixed with nectar (*amṛta*).

Having made it pleasing with canopies, white parasols, victory banners, flags, full vases, flowers, dance, song, music, and so forth—or whatever may be obtained— Please provide the text you would like translated. I am ready to assist you.

On an auspicious lunar day, weekday, asterism, and moment, having performed his bath and donned ornaments such as necklaces, anklets, armlets, earrings, bracelets, and rings—or whatever ornaments he has obtained—the Preceptor, who is the very form of Vajrasattva together with the Vidyā, should draw a double-circled square mandala in the center of that altar, featuring a universal lotus (*viśvābja*) and enclosed by a single line at its western gate, using colored powders (*rajas*), ointments, and so forth; or alternatively, he may draw it without archways (*toraṇa*).

On an auspicious day, lunar mansion, moment, and so forth, the preceptor—having bathed and adorned himself with necklaces, anklets, armlets, earrings, bracelets, finger-rings, and other ornaments, or adorned as they may be obtained—[enters] in the form of Vajrasattva together with the *vidyā* goddesses.

In the center of the pedestal, one should draw a multicolored lotus with a square grid of lines facing west, using colored powders or a paste made from rice flour and so forth; alternatively, there may be a second tier that is square but without archways (toraṇa).

On the front and other panels, one should place a wheel, a jewel, a lotus, and a sword; in the corners, Locanā, a vajra, a lotus, and an utpala; and in the center, a universal eight-petaled lotus. Upon that, on a pedestal marked with an eight-petaled lotus, covered by a cloth or the like, or on a lion throne, one should sit with the mental resolve (*adhimokṣa*) of being seated upon the pericarp of the bathing maṇḍala lotus—or, in the absence of a bathing maṇḍala, otherwise on a seat or similar support where the maṇḍala has been visualized—and there one should place the image, cloth painting, manuscript, shrine, or other object, facing either east or another direction.

On the eastern and other [sides] of the cloths are the wheel, jewel, lotus, and sword; in the intermediate directions are the eye, vajra, lotus, and utpala; and in the center is a multicolored eight-petaled lotus.

Upon that, one visualizes [the deity] being placed upon a lion throne—covered with a wooden seat inscribed with an eight-petaled lotus, or with cloth and so forth upon which a moon mandala has been drawn—atop the center of the lotus of the bathing mandala; or, even in the absence of a bathing mandala, it is likewise suchness.
Furthermore, on a meditation mandala such as a wooden seat and so forth, one should place images, cloth paintings, books, stūpas, and so on, facing either toward the east or in some other direction.

However, regarding those objects such as monasteries, shrines, perfumed chambers, and images that are not suitable for being moved to another location—one should resolve with firm conviction upon seeing their mandala as having the form of the previously visualized samayasattva; in such cases, there is no need for a bathing altar.

Furthermore, as for those such as temples, reliquaries, perfume chambers, and images that cannot be moved to another location, one should visualize them in the form of the *samayasattva* as before and cultivate firm conviction in the mandala; however, there is no need to arrange a bathing platform for them.

In either case, at the time of dusk, having placed an image or similar object before one and facing it, one should perform the *nīrājana* ceremony—either preceded by the offering of water for the feet (*pādya*), the respectful oblation (*argha*), and so forth, or even without such offerings.

In both instances, there is no fault; one should purify [the deity] by placing the image and so on in front, facing toward it, and performing the rite with or without the preliminary offering of the *arghya* and other substances.

There, having recited the mantra of Kuṇḍalin—*oṃ āḥ vighnāntakṛt hūṃ*—and the syllable *hūṃ* seven times over white mustard seeds held in the left and right fists respectively, one should sprinkle them twice each while circling counter-clockwise, reciting: *oṃ sarvapāpadahanavajrāya vajrasattvasya sarvapāpaṃ daha svāhā*. Having thus performed the ritual sprinkling (*nirmañcana*), one should cast the mustard seeds into the fire. Likewise, one should do so clockwise from the left to the right, and similarly with water.

Likewise, with white earthen bowls (*śarāva*), with cow-dung mixed with *dūrvā* sprouts, with balls of cooked rice (*bhakta-jaḍī*), and with the *śītalikā* rite; however, the earthen bowls and other such items must not be thrown into the fire.

Then, reciting the mantra of the *āvarta* (whirling), *oṃ āḥ vighnāntakṛta hūṃ*, and having recited the syllable *hūṃ* seven times, one should grasp [the vessel] with the right and left fists respectively. Reciting once for each, one should circumambulate it twice to the left, saying: *sarvapāpāṃ dahana vajrasattvasya sarvapāpaṃ daha svāhā*.

Reciting these words, one should cast the *argha* water onto the sacrificial ground while performing clockwise circumambulations; likewise, one should perform the same with water to the left and to the right. Similarly, one should do so with white conch shells, with pieces of cow dung together with sprouts of bamboo, and likewise with balls of rice together with lamps.
Likewise, it is also [permitted] for cotton cloths, provided that they are not thrown into the fire along with bowls and such.

Then, one should touch the image and so forth with both hands. With the mantra of the Lord of the Wheel (*cakreśa*), one should perform, as appropriate for the image or other object—whether it be the actual object or its reflection in a mirror—the smearing of fragrance upon the heart, the binding of the head with a garland of flowers, and the offering of *argha* water in front. Having whirled the lamp, one should fumigate it with incense made of resin mixed with ghee, over which the syllable *HŪṂ* has been recited seven times by means of the *kuṇḍalī*. This is the procedure for the *nīrājana* rite.

Then, some of them should touch the images and so forth with the mantra of the Lord of the Wheel (cakreśvara), applying fragrant ointment to the heart of the image and so forth—either directly or to its reflection appearing in a mirror—as appropriate.

Having bound a garland of poor-quality flowers and offered the water for the guest-offering (argha) in front, one should encircle [the object] with lamps and fumigate it with white incense mixed with ghee over which the syllable *hūṃ* has been recited seven times; this is the ritual of purification.

Thereafter, one should bathe the image or other object suitable for bathing with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*)—consisting of curd, milk, ghee, honey, and sugar-candy—which have been mixed together and placed in a copper vessel using a bundle of *dūrvā* grass over which the *kuṇḍali* mantra has been recited; and then with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*)—curd, milk, ghee, cow dung, and cow urine. One should anoint it with the mantra: *oṃ hūṃ trāṃ hrīḥ aḥ*. However, in the case of images painted on cloth, in books, or made of clay, one should bathe their reflection as it appears in a mirror.

Following that, with a small ladle rotated clockwise, one should wash the images and other objects that are worthy of purification—using the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), which consist of curd, milk, ghee, honey, and sugar mixed together and placed in a copper vessel, and subsequently using the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), namely cow’s milk, curd, ghee, dung, and urine—with the mantra: *oṃ hūṃ trāṃ hrīḥ āḥ*.

One should perform the anointing with this mantra. As for the painted cloth, the book, the [image] made of clay and so forth, or the painted images and the like, these refer to the reflections appearing in a mirror.

Then, having bathed [the image] with fragrant and pure water over which the *kuṇḍali* mantra has been recited, and having rubbed it dry with a paste made from the five barks of the five milk-trees—namely the *nyagrodha*, *udumbara*, *plakṣa*, *pippala*, and *gaṇḍamuṇḍa*—[one should recite]: *oṃ sarvatathāgatakāyaviśodhane svāhā*.

Reciting this mantra, having anointed [the image] with fragrant oil contained in a bronze vessel, rubbed it dry, and bathed it; having smeared it with *āmalaka* fruit placed in bronze and bathed it again; having smeared it with turmeric placed in bronze and bathed it again; and having anointed it with *śrīkhaṇḍa*, red sandalwood, saffron, *granthika*, and *aguru*—or as available, with saffron, *aguru*, musk, camphor, and so forth—[one visualizes it] being bathed by Tathāgatas and goddesses brought forth by the rays of the heart-seed syllable (*hṛdbīja*).

Preceded by auspicious songs, various musical instruments, and so forth, one should bathe [the deity] with the waters from the victory vase (*vijayakalaśa*) or others collected in a conch shell or elsewhere, while reciting the passage beginning with "Just as [beings] immediately after birth," which will be explained below. Having wiped away that residual water with a soft cloth, one should adorn [the deity] with garments and other ornaments according to one's capacity.

Then, having bathed with pure, fragrant water consecrated by the recitation of the *pradakṣiṇa* mantra, one should thoroughly anoint [the image] with a powder made from the bark of the five trees—*nyagrodha*, *udumbara*, *plakṣa*, *piśāca*, and *gandhamuṇḍa*—which have been placed in a vessel of *khadira* wood.

While reciting the mantra *oṃ sarvatathāgatakāyaviśodhane svāhā*, one should satisfy [the deity] by anointing it with fragrant sesame oil contained in a bronze vessel and then apply the *kyurura* (jujube) fruit residing in the bronze vessel. Having thus washed it, one should anoint it with mustard seeds from the bronze vessel and wash it again, using *śrīkhaṇḍa*, red sandalwood, and saffron.

Having anointed [the area] with whatever is available—such as *granthika*, *ākāru*, *gur-gum*, *ākāru*, *gla-tsi*, *ga-bur*, and so forth—one [should visualize] those [beings] summoned by the light rays of the seed-syllable at the heart.

While being bathed with the vases of the Tathāgatas and goddesses, preceded by auspicious songs and various musical instruments, one should perform the ritual bathing while reciting the verses beginning with "Just as at the moment of birth... and so forth, using the water from the *vijaya* vase and others poured into a conch shell or another vessel.
Having wiped the water from that [body] with soft clothing, one should adorn oneself with garments and so forth as much as possible.

Then, by means of the light rays from the heart-mantra, one should bring before oneself the wisdom-being (*jñānasattva*) to be installed and the deities such as the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas into the sky; having first offered the water for honoring (*argha*) and other gifts, with the right knee placed on the ground, sounding the bell with the left hand and offering incense with the right, one should utter "HŪṂ" with the vajra-tongue.

Then, with the light rays of the mantra at the heart, one should invite the wisdom beings (*jñānasattva*), the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and other deities into the space before oneself. Preceded by the offering of water for the feet and so forth, kneeling with the right knee on the ground, ringing the bell with the left hand and holding the incense burner with the right, one should visualize the tongue as a vajra produced from the syllable *hūṃ*.

O Blessed One, O such-and-such Sadvajra, King of Vidyās, homage be to you! O Compassionate Protector, I desire to perform your consecration for the sake of compassion toward the disciples and for your worship.

For the sake of increasing the merit of sentient beings and for the arising of the thought of awakening, O Blessed One, you ought to grant your grace to me, your devotee. May the Buddhas, who bestow the purpose of the wheel of activity for the world, attend to me.
Bodhisattvas established in the fruit, as well as other mantra-deities,
deities and world-protectors, spirits governed by perfect enlightenment,
beings who delight in the teaching, and others who possess the divine eye.
"I, [so-and-so], the Great Vajrī, shall perform the consecration of [so-and-so];
therefore, you ought to grant your presence."

"O Bhagavān, supreme Vajra, I bow to you, the King of Knowledge! Out of compassion for my disciples, and for the sake of making offerings to you, in order to increase the merit of sentient beings, and to generate the mind of awakening—O Protector whose very nature is compassion, I wish to perform your consecration. Therefore, O Bhagavān, I am full of devotion."

May those who have been granted the grace [of the teachings], the Buddhas who strive for the benefit of wandering beings, the Bodhisattvas established in the fruits, and whatever other deities of mantra there may be; the gods and the guardians of the world; the spirits who abide in the foundation of enlightenment; and all others who take great delight in the teaching and possess the vajra-eye—may they [all grant their blessing].
Please turn your true attention toward me! O Great Vajradharas, [I am] so-and-so; this is the consecration of so-and-so. Therefore, it is fitting that you all remain present here to perform it.
Thus one should recite three times.
Thus it should be recited three times.

Thus, with the words ending in "you are worthy here," one requests the consent (*adhivāsana*) for the purpose of consecration; then, having requested the presence (*saṃnidhāna*) by means of the remainder, and having fully worshipped, prostrated to, and praised the circle of deities situated in the sky, one should dismiss them with: *oṃ vajra punarāgamanāya muḥ*.

Thus, with the section ending in "rigs" (family), one requests the *adhiṣṭhāna* (empowerment) for the purpose of consecration; then, with the remainder, one requests the *upasthāna* (attendance). Having properly worshipped, prostrated to, and praised the circle of deities abiding in the sky, one should request their departure with: *oṃ vajrapuṇarāgamanaṃ yāmuḥ*.

Having bathed the image and others, and having anointed their heart, head, throat, and the tips of their arms, one should touch them three times with the right hand holding a vajra while reciting the Kuṇḍalī mantra; then one should mutter either the respective mantra or the Kuṇḍalī mantra, and offer the directional bali offerings.

Having thoroughly anointed the heart, crown, throat, hands, and the uṣṇīṣa of the consecrated images and so forth, and having made offerings, one should touch them three times with the right hand together with a vajra while reciting the *āvartana* mantra. Then, one should recite either one's own personal mantra or the *āvartana* mantra as appropriate, and also present the directional bali offerings.

However, for one who possesses firm conviction (*adhimokṣa*) regarding the consecration (*pratiṣṭhāpana*) of a deity even without performing the preliminary ritual of invocation (*adhivāsana*), that person may perform all the procedures—including the rite for invocation and those to be described for the consecration—on a single day, provided they do not perform the invocation itself. Nevertheless, rites such as the *nīrājana* (lustration) and others of a similar nature must be performed together at once. Even such a person, however, should certainly perform the invocation if the patron (*dānapati*) has the capacity to do so, for the sake of accumulating merit (*puṇya*). This is the procedure for the invocation of the deity.

In cases where the deity has not already been specially invoked (*adhivāsita*) but is being consecrated (*pratiṣṭhāpyate*), one must stabilize the superior resolve (*adhimukti*). Thus, the very fact that the deity has not been specially invoked is expressed for the purpose of the special invocation; all the words that will be explained for the purpose of the consecration are to be performed on a single day.

Furthermore, the concordant rituals such as purification and so forth should be performed only once and not repeated. In that regard, if the patron has the capacity, one should indeed perform the ritual of the *adhivāsana* (preliminary consecration) of the deity for the purpose of accumulating merit. This is the ritual of the *adhivāsana* of the deity.

Thereafter, at dawn, having had a beautiful bathing altar constructed, the preceptor—adorned with ornaments at an auspicious moment and embodying the form of Vajradhara together with his consort—should sit down and, preceded by offerings and worship, once again manifest the images and so forth established as before, as well as the monastery and other structures in their existing state, in the form of the *samayasattva*.

Following that, in the same manner as before, he should have a beautiful bathing platform constructed. Then, for a short while, the preceptor—adorned with ornaments and possessing the nature of Vajradhara together with Prajñā—should sit there. Preceded by the offering of *bali* and worship, he should likewise install the images and so forth.
One should generate the temples and other structures, exactly as they exist, in the form of the samayasattvas.

In that regard, concerning the tantras, the clear realizations (*abhisamaya*), the means of achievement (*sādhana*), and so forth, for whichever specific deity the sequence of arising is known, one should—immediately after emptiness—visualize its image either sequentially or instantaneously as having the form of the commitment being (*samayasattva*).

Furthermore, whatever specific deity is generated through the stages of the tantras, the clear realizations (*abhisamaya*), the *sādhana*s, and so forth—distinguished according to their respective types—that deity should be meditated upon in the form of the commitment-being (*samayasattva*), either sequentially or simultaneously, following the stage of emptiness in whatever manner is appropriate.

In the book [tradition], however, one should contemplate that immediately after the emptiness of the collection of syllables, Amitābha—embraced by Pāṇḍaravāsinī who arises from a red *hrīḥ* syllable on a red lotus and sun disk, which itself arises from a red *hrīḥ* syllable—transforms into the form of the assembled syllables; this is the *samayasattva*, appearing as a reflected image of Amitābha, who remains there.

As for the volumes [of scripture], they are the complete collection of syllables. Following the praise itself, from a red *hrīḥ* arising upon a red lotus and sun disk, there appears Amitābha, who has emerged from that same *hrīḥ* and is embraced by Pāṇḍaravāsinī; from the total transformation of him, the forms of the syllables arise.
One should contemplate that [the deity] abides as the commitment-being (samayasattva) in which the reflection of Amitābha has arisen.

Following the emptiness of the temple of Dīpaṅkara and so forth, upon a lotus and moon disc, from the syllable *bhrūṃ* arises an eight-spoked wheel, from which the syllable *bhrūṃ* transforms into Vairocana embraced by Locanā. Having transformed, he takes the form of Dīpaṅkara as a temple, a perfumed chamber (*gandhakuṭī*), or a reliquary (*caitya*). However, the temple is the reflected image of Vairocana together with his consort, abiding in the form of the *samayasattva*. In this manner, one should meditate on the perfumed chamber and the reliquary.

Regarding Dīpaṃkara, the temple, and so forth: following from emptiness, upon a lotus and moon disc, from a white syllable *bhrūṃ* arises an eight-spoked wheel; and from the syllable *bhrūṃ* arises Vairocana embraced by Locanā, who then takes the form of Dīpaṃkara, or the form of a temple, or the form of a perfumed chamber.

It is in the form of a stūpa. Furthermore, the temple exists as the form of the Samayasattva, appearing as the image of Vairocana together with Prajñā; likewise, one should meditate upon the perfume chamber and the stūpa in the same way.
Having thus generated the *samayasattva*, one should perform the purification as before,
preceded by the offering of the water for the feet (*argha*) and so forth.

Then, having performed the anointing with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) and so forth according to the procedure just described—extending from the smearing with saffron and other substances to the bathing and the removal of clinging water—one enters the maṇḍala house. Having placed the image or other object facing the maṇḍala in the northeast direction of the maṇḍala, or in another location nearby where there is no space, keeping it steady; or, in the case of a monastery and the like, leaving it in its own place as appropriate; one should first perform the meditative cultivation of the empowerment of the heart-seed syllable, the eyes, the body, and so forth.

Having performed the rites previously described—such as the summoning of the *jñānasattva* and so forth—by means of the rays from the seed-syllable in one’s own heart according to the respective [deity], and having recited three times the passage beginning with "O Blessed One" and ending with "you are worthy," one should, as appropriate, draw in the deities by means of the heart-rays, cause the *jñānasattva* to enter its corresponding *samayasattva*, unify them into a single flavor, and bring [the deity] under control. || O ||

Then, immediately following that, having performed the rites just described—such as anointing with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), applying saffron (*kuṅkuma*) and other substances, bathing, and wiping away the water used for washing—the practitioner should lead [the disciple] into the mandala house; he should be placed in the northeastern corner (*īśāna-kona*) of the mandala, or, if there is no space there, in another location as appropriate.

Furthermore, one should place images and so forth facing toward the mandala, but not too far away. As for those [images] such as temples that cannot be moved, they should remain exactly where they are located.

Having first performed the meditation on the blessing of their seed-syllables at the heart, as well as their eyes and so forth, and their bodies and so forth, according to what is appropriate, one should immediately carry out the previously mentioned procedures, such as inviting the wisdom-being (*jñānasattva*) who is identical to oneself, by means of the light rays from the seed-syllable at one's own heart.

Recite three times from "Bhagavān" up to "kula," and as appropriate, having summoned the wisdom being (jñānasattva) through the light rays of the deities at one's heart, one should cause it to enter the commitment being (samayasattva) who is oneself, making them of one taste and bringing them under control.

Then, having invoked the Tathāgatas residing in the ten directions and the goddesses such as Locanā into the space before him by means of light rays from the seed-syllable in his own heart, and having worshipped them for the sake of consecrating the images and so forth— *Then, by means of the light rays from the seed-syllable in one’s own heart, one invites the Tathāgatas residing in the ten directions and the goddesses such as Locanā into the space before one; having worshipped them, [one does so] for the purpose of consecrating the statues and so forth.*
Just as Guṇākara was given the consecration by the Vajra-holder for the protection of the world, so indeed should you grant it to him.
Just as the Vajra-holder bestowed empowerment upon the Buddha for the sake of protecting wandering beings, bestowing it as a source of qualities, so too, please bestow it upon this person.
One should supplicate with this verse.
With these words, one should offer this verse of supplication.

And by those Tathāgatas, having entered into meditative absorption through wisdom and melted by great passion, [they enter] through their own *vairocana* gate, exit via the *vajra* path, and—having been poured out through the mouths of the goddesses' lotuses by those fluids—consecrate the images and so forth; then, emerging from the lotuses again in the forms of the arms, faces, and other limbs, they remain filling the external sky together with the *vidyā*-consorts such as Locanā.

With white jars filled with the nectar of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), which are adorned with hands like tender sprouts and surrounded by showers of parasols, banners, flags, dance, song, instrumental music, flowers, saffron, and so forth; [one should visualize] that image and the rest emerging from the lotus and being consecrated by Rūpavajrā and the others, while auspicious songs such as "That which is auspicious... (to be mentioned below) are offered by the Yoginīs, or one should oneself sing those songs, using the water from each of the Vijayā and other jars individually, or combined together in a single conch shell.
In due order, by means of the nectar-like bodhicitta held in the hand of the Vajra with sprouts and flowing from the tip of the vajra with sprouts,
even the Tathāgatas, having melted through great passion upon entering into meditative equipoise with Prajñā, enter through their own path of Vairocana.

Those essences (khu ba) extracted through the vajra path empower the images and so forth as they enter from the mouth into the lotus; then, having been drawn back out from the lotus in the form of faces, hands, and so on, they dwell filling the entirety of space together with the consorts of the families, such as Locanā and the others, amidst parasols, victory banners, dance, song, and the sound of musical instruments.

While a rain of incense, flowers, saffron, and so forth is falling, and with hands holding slightly tilted white vases filled with the nectar of bodhicitta, they confer empowerment upon the physical forms and other objects as they emerge from the lotuses; and [this is performed] by Rūpavajrā and the others.

While the yoginīs sing auspicious songs beginning with "Whatever auspiciousness... and I myself likewise sing them, one pours together the water from the *vijaya* (victory) and other vases into a single vessel and places it within the *duddha* (milk) [vessel].
In due order, even with each individual [finger], one should hold a vajra together with its petals in the hand; from its tip, the nectar of bodhicitta flows down.
Just as all the Tathāgatas were bathed immediately upon birth,
so shall I bathe this one with pure, divine water.
Just as all the Tathāgatas are bathed by the mere touch of water, so too do I perform this bath with pure divine water.

Oṃ āḥ [sarvatathāgatā]bhiṣekasamayaśriye hūṃ svāhā | Oṃ vajrodakābhiṣiñca hūṃ | Reciting this, one should perform the consecration with firm conviction, thinking: "The Blessed Lord Vajrasattva himself, the supreme guru in the form of the presiding deity of the maṇḍala, is consecrating and bathing me. This is the water consecration (udakābhiṣeka). ||o||

Reciting: *oṃ āḥ sarvatathāgatābhiṣekasamaya huṃ svāhā | oṃ vajrodaka abhiṣiñca huṃ*, one should perform the water empowerment by firmly resolving that the Blessed One Vajrasattva himself enters the form of the sublime guru, the lord of the maṇḍala, and bestows the consecration through the ritual bath. This is the water empowerment.

Reciting "Oṃ Āḥ Vajrābhiṣiñca Hūṃ," the Guru—being the Lord of the Maṇḍala and Vajradhara himself—with firm conviction, places upon the head of the deity in the image and so forth a crown made of jewels, cloth, and other materials, empowered by the five Tathāgatas. This is the Crown Empowerment (*mukuṭābhiṣeka*). Furthermore, for a hero (*vīra*), one should also bind a turban on the forehead with the mantra "Oṃ Hūṃ Trāṃ Hrīḥ Aḥ."
The head-ornament made of precious gems, cotton cloth, and so forth, blessed by the five Tathāgatas: Oṃ Āḥ.

Reciting "Vajrābhiṣiñca Hūṃ," one should visualize that the Guru himself, in the form of the Lord of the Maṇḍala, performs the donning; thus, one should firmly believe that it is being placed upon the heads of the deities in the form of the statues and so forth. This is the crown initiation (*mukuṭābhiṣeka*). For the Hero (*vīra*), a silk ribbon (*darpaṭṭa*) should be tied to the forehead with the mantra "Oṃ Hūṃ Trāṃ Hrīḥ Āḥ."
Today you have been consecrated by the Buddhas through the vajra-consecration;
take this state of all-buddhahood, the vajra, for the sake of perfect accomplishment.
"By means of the vajra empowerment of all the Buddhas, you are empowered this very day. This is for the sake of fully accomplishing the state of all the Buddhas; therefore, hold the vajra."

Reciting thus, one should offer the vajra through resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), thinking that Vajrasattva himself is indeed offering it; and through the conviction that it has been accepted by the deity of the image and so forth, this is the vajra initiation (*vajrābhiṣeka*).

Reciting thus, one should focus [the vajra] with the firm conviction that Vajrasattva himself is bestowing it in that very manner. Furthermore, one should maintain the firm conviction that it is being held by the deities of the physical forms and so forth; this is the vajra empowerment.

Reciting, "Oṃ, I consecrate you as the Lord of Vajras; remain, O Vajra, you are the Samaya," one should present the bell with such focused conviction (*adhimukti*). Through the firm conviction that it has been grasped by the deity of the image and so forth, this is the bell-consecration (*ghaṇṭābhiṣeka*).

Reciting: *oṃ vajrādhivati svāṃ abhiṣiñcāmi tiṣṭha vajrasattva*, one should thus entrust the bell with intense devotion. Furthermore, the visualization that the deity of the physical form and so forth is to be grasped [by the disciple] is the empowerment of the bell.

"Oṃ, Vajrasattva, I consecrate you with the vajra-name consecration. Oṃ, [you are] such-and-such-vajra. Reciting thus, while resolving that he is indeed Vajrasattva and bestowing the name upon the deity of the image and so forth according to its own specific name, one should utter it; this is the name-consecration (nāmābhiṣeka).

Reciting “oṃ vajrasattva tvām abhiṣiñcāmi vajranāmābhiṣekataḥ oṃ che ge mo vajrasattva,” one should likewise address Vajrasattva himself—upon the physical form and so forth—with the firm conviction that one is bestowing the name upon oneself exactly as it is; this is the name empowerment (*nāmābhiṣeka*).

Having visualized the deity of the image and so forth performing the gesture of embracing with the knowledge-mudrā (jñānamudrā) while holding a vajra and vajra-bell in his hands, one should consecrate them by means of the water-consecration procedure mentioned immediately above and seal them on the head with the Lord of their respective family (*kuleśa*). However, those whose family is unknown should be sealed with Akṣobhya or Vajrasattva. Other Tathāgatas, Bodhisattvas, and Goddesses should be made to enter that very form of the Knowledge-being (*jñānasattva*), and one should empower [the image] with the mantra: *oṃ supratiṣṭhitavajre svāhā*.

With the mantra *oṃ hūṃ hrīḥ bhrūṃ khaṃ vajrībhava dṛḍhaṃ tiṣṭha bhrūṃ khaṃ*, one consecrates the monastery and the *caitya*; for the book, however, with the two mantras *oṃ supratiṣṭhitavajre svāhā* and *oṃ hūṃ hrīḥ tvaṃ*. Thus is the master’s initiation (*ācāryābhiṣeka*).

One should visualize that the hands, holding a vajra and bell, perform the manner of embracing with the wisdom-mudrā; immediately thereafter, one is consecrated through the ritual of the water empowerment as just described, and the crown of the head is sealed by the lord of one’s respective family. For those whose family is unknown, they should be sealed by Akṣobhya or Vajrasattva.

The Tathāgatas, bodhisattvas, and other goddesses are then introduced there as the nature of the wisdom beings (*jñānasattva*) and consecrated with the mantra: *oṃ supratiṣṭha vajre svāhā*. For temples and stūpas, however, it is done with the mantra: *oṃ hūṃ hrīḥ bhrūṃ khaṃ vajribhavādhiṣṭha bhrūṃ khaṃ*.
Regarding the book, it is with the mantras "oṃ supratiṣṭha vajre svāhā" and "oṃ hūṃ hrīḥ trāṃ" that [the empowerment is conferred]; this is the master’s empowerment (ācāryābhiṣeka).

Thereafter, desiring the increase of the merit of the donor (*dānapati*) in accordance with the form of the image, one should open the eyes of the image while reciting: "Oṃ cakṣuś cakṣuḥ samantacakṣurviśodhane svāhā," applying collyrium with a gold rod no smaller than a *māṣaka* in weight, which has been smeared with ghee and honey placed within a silver *mallikā* vessel.

Following that, in accordance with the image and so forth, and in conformity with the desire of the donor who wishes to increase merit, one should perform the eye-opening ceremony for the image using an ointment applied with a golden spoon to a silver vessel containing butter and honey, while reciting: *oṃ cakṣuścakṣuḥ samantacakṣur viśodhane svāhā*. Thus, the eyes of the image should be opened with the medicinal ointment.

And for the sake of pacification and other purposes, one should resolve that the presiding deity (adhidevatā) of the book and so forth—who has been visualized as reflected in a mirror—is intent upon beholding the donor and others. Regarding books and the like, one should have firm conviction that the deities are present in their reflections visualized within a mirror; for the purpose of pacifying [illnesses] and so forth, one should regard them as the supreme deity who gazes upon the patron and others.
Then, one should show the mirror with the mantra: *oṃ vajrasattva āḥ*. One should also perform everything, such as the shooting of arrows and so forth, through meditative visualization.

% NB the order is different from the VĀ % Then, one should show the mirror with the mantra *oṃ vajrasattva āḥ*. One should meditate on the shooting of arrows and so forth; all [these] abide accordingly.

Thereafter, one should contemplate as follows: Vajrasattva, in the form of the Lord of the Mandala (Cakreśa), causes the assembly of Tathāgatas such as Vairocana together with their consorts—summoned by rays from the seed-syllable in his own heart—to enter through the door of Vairocana. Having experienced the state of melting into great bliss (*mahāsukha*), he emits the form of bodhicitta from the vajra and lotus and causes it to enter the mouth of the deity of the image and so forth. This is the secret initiation (*guhyābhiṣeka*).

Following that, by means of the light rays from the seed syllable at his own heart, the assembly of Tathāgatas such as Vairocana, together with their consorts, is drawn in through the gateway of Cakreśvara-vajradhara; having been dissolved, they experience great bliss.

One should visualize that the essence of bodhicitta, emanated from the mouths of the vajra and lotus, is poured into the mouths of the deities, such as the [central] image; this is the secret empowerment.

Then, one should resolve that the deity of the image and so forth—having entered into union with the goddess presented by the Vajra-holder—is composed of innate bliss (*sahajānanda*). [Thus is the initiation of the knowledge of wisdom (*prajñājñānābhiṣeka*).]

Then, by entering into union with the goddess sent by that Vajradhara, one should cultivate conviction that the deities of the physical form and so forth are of the nature of innate joy; this is the wisdom-knowledge empowerment (prajñājñānābhiseka).

Thereafter, one should resolve with conviction that the deity of the image and so forth—whose nature has been imparted by that Vajrasattva as the fourth consecration—is the single essence of emptiness and compassion consisting of great bliss, in which all obscurations along with their habitual tendencies have been abandoned; this is the fourth consecration.

Following that, one should resolve with conviction that the deities of the physical forms and so forth, which possess the nature of the fourth empowerment as taught by Vajrasattva, are the great bliss in which emptiness and compassion are of one taste, having abandoned the obscurations along with their habitual tendencies; this is the fourth empowerment.

Alternatively, with these mantras: *oṃ āḥ vajravāsase hūṃ svāhā* | *oṃ āḥ vajrapuṣpe hūṃ svāhā* | *oṃ āḥ vajradhūpe hūṃ svāhā* | *oṃ āḥ vajradīpe hūṃ svāhā* | *oṃ āḥ vajranaivedye hūṃ svāhā* | *oṃ āḥ vajragandhe hūṃ svāhā* | *oṃ sarvābharaṇavibhūṣaṇe svāhā*. The mantra for sprinkling various items such as fruits and flowers is: *oṃ āḥ sarvasaṃśodhani hūṃ phaṭ*. The mantra for offering fruit is: *oṃ jraṃ svāhā*.

Alternatively: oṃ āḥ vajra vāsase hūṃ svāhā | oṃ āḥ vajra puṣpe hūṃ svāhā | oṃ āḥ vajra dhūpe hūṃ svāhā | oṃ āḥ vajra dīpe hūṃ svāhā | oṃ āḥ vajra naivedye hūṃ svāhā | oṃ āḥ vajra gandhe hūṃ svāhā | oṃ sarva-āvaraṇaviśodhani hūṃ svāhā ||

By means of these mantras: *oṃ āḥ sarvaśāśodhane hūṃ phaṭ*—this is the secret mantra for various substances such as fruit and victory banners. *oṃ vajrasvāhā*—this is the mantra for offering the fruit.

Thereafter, having performed the nourishing rite (*āpyāyana*) by means of a *śāntika* fire-oblation according to the procedure to be described, one should prepare the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) in the fire of the oblation-pit, or, in its absence, in another fire. Then, having offered that milk-rice (*pāyasa*) along with the pledge-substance (*samayadravya*) and yellow pigment (*rocanā*), one should recite the mantra: "Oṃ, to the divine food, which satisfies through meditative absorption and visualization, svāhā! While reciting this, one should cause the deity—visualized as a reflected image within the statue, book, or other object—to consume it.

Thereafter, one should offer water for sipping (ācamana), sandalwood paste and so forth, and betel leaf mixed with aromatic powder. Then, one should cause [the disciple] to hear the pledge (samaya) by reciting: *oṃ hūṃ trāṃ hrīḥ aḥ*.

Following that, having satisfied [the deity] with a peaceful fire offering (śāntihoma) according to the ritual to be explained, one should prepare a meal of *tsāru* in the sacrificial fire of the homa, or if that is unavailable, in any other fire. Subsequently, one should offer milk-rice (*pāyasa*), the substances of the commitment (*samayadravya*), and the water-offering (*argha*). Oṃ divya agne samādhiye nirmāṇe svāhā.

Reciting this mantra, one should cause the deities—the reflected images that have arisen through meditation upon the physical forms, books, and so forth—to partake of the offering. Then, having offered water for rinsing the mouth, sandalwood powder, and tooth-cleansing sticks, one should proclaim the commitment (*samaya*) with: *oṃ hūṃ trāṃ hrīḥ āḥ*.

Then, having caused Amitābha together with Prajñā to enter the syllables within the book, one should contemplate him in the form of syllables; and having caused Vairocana together with Vidyā to enter the monastery or the caitya, one should contemplate him in the form of the monastery, as the support for the Perfect Buddha, his Dharma, the Bodhisattvas, the Śrāvakas, and so forth, as the abode of various meditative absorptions, in the form of the caitya, empowered by Vajrasattva and others, for the sake of benefiting the world until the end of saṃsāra.

Then, having placed Amitābha together with Prajñā into the letters of the volumes, they take the form of the letters; and having placed Vairocana together with the Vidyā, they place them within the temples or stūpas. The form of the temple consists of the representations of the Perfect Buddha, his Dharma, the Bodhisattvas, the Śrāvakas, and so forth.

One should visualize that the bases of the various meditative concentrations and the forms of the stūpas have been blessed by Vajrasattva and the others, in order to accomplish the welfare of migratory beings for as long as cyclic existence endures.
Then, having removed the flowers and other offerings, with palms joined in reverence:
*de nas me tog la sogs pa phul te thal mo sbyar nas |*
Just as all the perfectly awakened ones reside in Tuṣita,
so may they likewise abide here in this image within the womb of Queen Māyā.
Remaining here eternally as my protector, accept these offerings and so forth for the sake of [the disciple named] so-and-so, in order to increase their bodhicitta.

Just as all the Perfect Buddhas, having resided in Tuṣita, entered the womb of the goddess Māyā, so too may you reside within this image. May the Protector dwell here eternally; for the sake of increasing the mind of awakening, please accept these offerings of flowers and the like for the benefit of [Name].

Having thus entreated for long-term stability, and reciting the *kuṇḍali* mantra, one should encircle the lower, middle, and upper parts of the image or other object three times with the vajra held in the right hand—drawn upward and curved—and thereby make it firm.

Having thus offered this prayer for the sake of long-term endurance, one should recite the *āvartana-mantra* and, circling three times with the right hand brandishing a vajra, stabilize [the image] by moving it beneath, between, and above the statue and so forth:
*Akṣobhyavajra mahājñāna vajradhātu mahābudha | Trimaṇḍala trivajrāgra ghoṣavajra namo 'stu te ||*
Vairocana, great purity, vajra-peace, great delight;
O supreme among those whose nature is luminous, homage be to you, Vajra of the [ten] directions!
O King of Jewels, most profound, vajra-like space,
stainless, pure by nature, untainted— homage be to you, Vajra Body!
O Vajrāmita, great king, free from conceptual construction, bearer of the space-vajra;
you who have attained the perfection of passion, O Bhāṣavajra, homage be to you!
O Amoghavajra, perfectly awakened one, fulfiller of all hopes,
born of the nature of purity, Vajrasattva, homage be to you!

Akṣobhya-vajra of great primordial wisdom, Great Sage of the Vajra Realm, Supreme Three-Vajras of the three maṇḍalas—to you, O Vajra Realm, I prostrate! Vairocana of great purity, Vajra of peace and great bliss, Supreme of the supreme, naturally luminous—O Teacher, Vajra, to you I prostrate! King of Jewels, most profound...

Vajra sky, stainless space, Pure by nature and unstained— I prostrate to you, Vajra Body! Great King, immeasurable Vajra, Holder of the non-conceptual Vajra of space, Attainer of the perfection of passion— I prostrate to you, Vajra Speech! Amoghasiddhi, perfect Buddha, Who completely fulfills all intentions.
Arisen from the nature of purity, homage to you, Vajrasattva!

Having praised with these verses, one should recite the hundred-syllable mantra— beginning with *oṃ vajrasattva samayam anupālaya*— three times in order to pacify defects such as omissions in the ritual procedure.
*Through non-attainment, through lack of knowledge, and through incapacity, O Compassionate One,*
Whatever has been done deficiently or otherwise, you ought to forgive all of that.

Whatever has not been obtained, whatever has not been fully understood, and whatever has been interrupted through incapacity—as well as whatever other faults have been committed—all these you should forgive out of compassion.
Having thus requested forgiveness.

The Fully Awakened Ones, the goddesses, and their sons, as well as the deities beginning with Brahmā and the nāgas, ought to forgive whatever deficiency in the ritual procedure or other such errors may have occurred.
May Agni, Earth, Water, and Wind protect this image for a long time;
may they bring peace, prosperity, and well-being in every way to the lord of donors.
May his sons, his disciples, and we ourselves then go joyfully to the realm of the Buddha, in order to return here once more.

I ask the Perfectly Enlightened One, the goddesses, their sons, Brahmā and the others, and all the gods and *nāgas* to forgive whatever ritual procedures were incomplete or otherwise deficient. May the fire, water, earth, and wind protect this image for a long time. May the patrons, their children and so forth, the disciples, and I myself—none of us having committed any fault—be protected in every way.
I pray that you perform pacification, enrichment, and auspiciousness; even after you have departed for the Buddha-fields, I pray that you return once again.
Having thus requested three times, one should offer the directional bali offerings and the bali for all beings.
Thus, one should supplicate three times and present the directional torma offerings as well as the torma for all elemental spirits.
The patron, having likewise performed circumambulation, worship, and prostration before the image and so forth, should satisfy the preceptor with appropriate ritual fees.
The patron, having performed circumambulations, offerings, and prostrations before the image and so forth, should also fully satisfy the preceptor with authentic gifts.

In this case, a book should be consecrated in a maṇḍala where Amitābha is the presiding deity; however, in one where Vairocana is the presiding deity, a monastery or similar structure should be consecrated. In a maṇḍala where Akṣobhya or Vajrasattva is the presiding deity, all images may be consecrated even if their family (kula) is unknown. Alternatively, whichever family is known for a particular image-deity, that image should be placed in a maṇḍala where the Tathāgata of that family is the presiding deity.

Here, in the maṇḍala of the principal deity Amitābha, the book is to be consecrated; in the case of the principal deity Vairocana, it is the temple and so forth; and in the case of the principal deity Akṣobhya or Vajrasattva, all images and even those whose lineage is unknown are to be consecrated.
Alternatively, if one knows which family a particular deity belongs to, [one should enter] the primary maṇḍala of the Tathāgata of that family.
In some cases, however,
whatever image is to be installed should have its maṇḍala prepared according to the tantra in which it is established; or else, [the maṇḍala] of one's own personal deity should be made.

"Whatever belongs to the preceptor, one should treat it with a view toward [avoiding] division. Thus it is said: "In whatever form the consecration is to be performed, and whichever tantra establishes it, therein one should construct its maṇḍala; or else, regarding one's own *iṣṭadevatā*—whatever belongs to the preceptor himself—one should perceive it as being distinct [from others]."

In this context, "of that" refers to the *bimba* (the visualized form) by virtue of its being the presiding lord of the maṇḍala. "His own deity" means the Tathāgata who is the lord of the family (*kula*) of that *bimba*; for him, this maṇḍala should be constructed. Alternatively, the master’s own personal maṇḍala should be constructed. For whatever he meditates upon, that indeed belongs to him. Thus, three positions have been stated. By this, it is established that even when such a maṇḍala is described in one tantra, the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) of deities mentioned in other tantras is appropriate, because the maṇḍalas of those families are subsumed within the maṇḍalas of the principal lords as they have been described. ||o||

Regarding the phrase "of that" (*tasya*) here, it refers to the physical form (*vigraha*), which is precisely the Lord of the Maṇḍala himself. "One's own *adhidaiva*" is the Tathāgata who is the Lord of the family (*gotra*) of that form; in this context, one should construct his maṇḍala. Alternatively, the master himself should construct his own maṇḍala. Thus, three positions are stated: "that which he meditates upon is precisely this."

In such a maṇḍala described by means of the ritual procedures taught in any other tantra as well, it is appropriate to perform the consecration of deities taught in other tantras; for the very maṇḍala of the principal deity as it has been taught subsumes all the maṇḍalas belonging to its respective family.

In the *Saṃkṣiptapratiṣṭhā* (Concise Consecration), however, immediately after the emptiness [of the image and so forth], one should instantaneously manifest that respective Samayasattva, empowered with the eyes, body, and so on; then, having internalized within it the Jñānasattva brought by rays from the seed-syllable in one’s own heart, and having had it consecrated by the Tathāgatas and others brought by rays from the seed-syllable in one’s own heart, and having consecrated oneself with the water from the flask, worshipped it, and recited its mantra one hundred and eight times—the image and so forth become consecrated.

The concise consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) is as follows: having generated the blessing of the eyes, body, and so forth of the respective pledge-being (*samayasattva*) in each [image] and so on, instantaneously following upon their emptiness, one causes the respective wisdom-being (*jñānasattva*) to enter it, summoned by the light rays of the seed-syllable at one’s own heart.

The Tathāgatas and others, summoned by the light rays from the seed-syllable at one's own heart, bestow empowerment; then, having also empowered oneself with the water from the vase and made offerings, one should recite its mantra one hundred and eight times. By this, the consecration of the physical image and so forth is accomplished.

When, however, a special honor for the *tathāgatadhātu* (relic-element) is desired, then at the very time of construction, one should have a cavity made in the head or on the pedestal of the image, or within the interior of a *caitya*. Once it is completed, [one should write] upon birch bark with saffron and *gorocanā*: *Namo bhagavate śākyamunaye tathāgatāyārhate samyaksambuddhāya | tadyathā | oṃ mune 2 mahāmunaye svāhā |* *Ye dharmā hetuprabhavā hetuṃ teṣāṃ tathāgato hy avadat |*

And he who teaches the cessation of these is the Great Śramaṇa. Having thus written this specific dhāraṇī, one should wrap the consecrated relic (dhātu) and, reciting "Oṃ, to the womb of the mantra-relic, svāhā," cast it into the cavity. Thereafter, while muttering "Oṃ, to the womb of the Vajradhātu, svāhā," one should seal the entrance of the cavity with adamantine paste (vajralepa) and perform its consecration as previously described.

Whenever one wishes to perform a special act of veneration for the relics of the Tathāgata, at that very time of accomplishment, one should fashion an image with its head or back hollowed out like a stūpa; once it is completed, with yellow orpiment and vermilion on birch bark, [one should write]: *Namo bhagavate śākyamunaye tathāgatāyārhate samyaksaṃbuddhāya. Tadyathā:*...

Having written this specific dhāraṇī: *oṃ mu ni mu ni mu h’a mu na ye svāhā | ye dharmā hetu prabhavā hetun teṣāṃ tathāgato hy avadat | teṣāṃ ca yo nirodha evaṃvādī mahāśramaṇaḥ*, wrap it around the bone of one who has been washed. Then, while reciting *oṃ mantra dhātu garbhāya svāhā*, place it within the emptiness.
Reciting "oṃ vajradhātugarbhāya svāhā," one should close the door of emptiness with the vajra-enclosure and perform the consecration as before.

Others, however, maintain that even for an image of Saṃvara, Hevajra, and so forth, there must indeed be consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) through the entry into the gnosis-maṇḍala (*jñānamaṇḍala*) and the initiation following the generation of the *samayasattva* of the *Samāja*. They argue that since the *Guhyasamāja* is unsurpassed, immediately thereafter the Lord of the *Samāja* Gnosis-Maṇḍala should be manifested in the form of Saṃvara and the others; thus, the image itself takes on that very form—wherein lies the contradiction? || o ||

In other cases, even for the physical forms of Hevajra, Cakrasaṃvara, and so forth, they become consecrated precisely through the generation of the Saṃvara samayas, the entry of the wisdom maṇḍala, and the conferral of empowerment; this is because the *Guhyasamāja* is unsurpassed.

Immediately following that, one should clearly visualize the lords of the mandalas of the samaya-beings and wisdom-beings who have just gathered as the forms of Cakrasaṃvara and so forth; for how could their physical forms be contradictory to those very forms? Thus it was said.

In the consecration of knowledge (*vidyā-pratiṣṭhā*), the preceptor should visualize himself as the form of Vajradhara or the form of a Knowledge-Lord (*vidyādhipati*); therein, he should perform the entry of the Knowledge-Being (*jñānasattva*) and so forth according to the ritual procedure.

In the same way, according to the circumstances, one should incorporate the specific object of the rite (*sādhya*)—whether the practitioner or another—and the Lord of the Vidyā into the mantra along with one's own name. Having caused the Vidyā to enter through the upper aperture or the mouth, and having led her who has emerged via the path of the *vajra* into the lotus of the deity, one should perform the consecration: first by the Tathāgatas summoned by the rays of light from the seed-syllable in the heart, who have entered in that manner; then, once they have gone outside, one should sprinkle her as she is being consecrated externally with water from the flask. Having performed worship, one should recite the heart-mantra of the Lord of the Vidyā one hundred and eight times. This is the ritual procedure for the consecration of a Vidyā.

Regarding the consecration of the *vidyā*: having fashioned the form of the Master Vajradhara or the form of the *vidyā*-lord, one should meditate upon the entry of the *vidyā*-lord and his wisdom-being (*jñānasattva*) into the *vidyā*, according to the ritual procedures as they are. Likewise, the specific details of the object to be accomplished should be applied as appropriate. Then, the *vidyā*-lord [is associated] with the mantras.

Having inserted the names of those to be accomplished [into the mantra], one inserts them through the aperture or the mouth of the Vidyā’s crown and emits them through the vajra-path; they enter the lotus of the goddess. Then, the Tathāgatas summoned by the light rays from the heart enter [the body] in that manner. While they are conferring empowerment, those who have been emitted [from the lotus] are empowered by the water of the vase as they emerge.

One should perform the empowerment; having made perfect offerings, one should recite the heart-mantra of the Lord of Vidyās one hundred and eight times. This is the ritual for the consecration of a Vidyā.
